items.summary: Language models cannot inherently interact with external enterprise environments such as code repositories, incident reports, or production logs without software interfaces. An AI agent functions by using a language model to evaluate a task and iteratively select appropriate tools to execute. The host application runs the selected tool, returns the output to the language model, and allows the model to decide subsequent actions. Tools range from read-only data retrieval to state-changing actions, ultimately determining an agent's operational capabilities. While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized protocol for discovering and invoking tools via operations like tools/list and tools/call, it does not address enterprise-specific governance. DoorDash's Agent Gateway architecture mediates interactions between AI agents and downstream MCP servers by separating traffic handling from configuration. The gateway comprises two core components: a proxy operating on the data plane and a registry serving as the control plane. The proxy authenticates callers, enforces permissions and rate limits, attaches credentials, and audits requests, while the registry maintains metadata, policies, and tool catalogs. Additionally, DoorDash partitions internal and external workflows into separate proxy planes to maintain isolated trust boundaries.

items.title: Why Do LLMs Lie?
items.summary: Hallucination in large language models refers to generated information that is factually incorrect, invented, or inconsistent with expected source material. A response does not have to be entirely false to be considered a hallucination; even a single fabricated detail within an otherwise useful answer qualifies. While hallucinations resemble confident falsehoods, they differ from lies because models lack the intent to deceive. Ultimately, whether generated fiction constitutes a hallucination depends heavily on context and what the output claims to represent. AI support assistant errors can be categorized into three overlapping types: factual hallucinations, faithfulness hallucinations, and fabrications. A factual hallucination contradicts reality, whereas a faithfulness hallucination contradicts the provided source documents. Fabrication involves inventing details or entities entirely, often acting as a subtype of factuality failure. Consequently, an AI assistant can be completely faithful to an outdated document while still producing a factually incorrect answer regarding current reality. Large language models generate responses by iteratively predicting and selecting the most likely next token based on calculated probabilities. During the pretraining phase, model parameters internalize linguistic patterns, conceptual associations, and structures from large amounts of text. However, generating statistically probable continuations is fundamentally distinct from verifying factual claims. Consequently, models can convincingly mimic authoritative language and structured formats—such as citations or specific policy terms—without factual grounding.

items.summary: The internet was originally designed around the assumption of human users, but automated systems now generate the majority of web traffic as AI shifts toward autonomous agents. Despite this evolution, web payment interfaces remain human-centric, creating friction for automated transactions. The Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) resolves this issue by providing an interface tailored for AI agents to negotiate and execute payments across the web. This development marks a transition toward fully automated transactions where humans are removed from the payment process entirely. Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) is a protocol designed to standardize automated payments between software agents without human intervention. Co-authored by Stripe and Tempo, MPP establishes a framework using HTTP headers to communicate payment challenges, credentials, and receipts. The specification has been published as the Payment HTTP Authentication Schema and submitted to the IETF. By decoupling payment methods across different rails like card networks and blockchains, MPP aims to enable any agent to autonomously buy from any service without prior integration. The Machine Payment Protocol (MPP) framework allows autonomous agents to access paid APIs on demand without prior account creation or API key provisioning. When an agent requests a resource, the server responds with an HTTP 402 Payment Required status and a challenge outlining the payment terms. The agent verifies the terms against pre-configured spending limits on a delegated key and retries the request with a single-use payment credential. Once verified, the server delivers the resource and a receipt header, allowing rails like Stripe to process payments via PaymentIntent objects without creating persistent user records.

items.title: How to Customize a Model to Learn New Tricks
items.summary: Prompting provides an accessible starting point for customizing model behavior by specifying tasks, constraints, and examples via few-shot prompting. When external or updated knowledge is required, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant context dynamically at inference time without altering model weights. However, when models exhibit recurring behavioral weaknesses or handling many examples bloats request inputs, fine-tuning modifies the model's learned parameters directly. While fine-tuning embeds desired behaviors into the model itself, RAG remains preferable for frequently changing data or requirements needing verifiable external traceability. Fine-tuning builds upon pre-existing language model capabilities by updating numerical parameters on focused datasets, reducing the training required for specialization. Common approaches include supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for direct input-response mapping and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to refine behaviors through ranked outputs and reward models. While full fine-tuning adjusts every parameter across the network, it demands substantial GPU memory for tracking weights, updates, and activations. Parameter-efficient techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA address these resource constraints by adapting models without requiring every parameter to be independently updated. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that keeps a base model's original weights frozen while attaching small trainable components called adapters to internal calculations. These adapters utilize two compact matrices to compute adjustments that are added directly to the model's internal processing rather than rewriting finished outputs. By learning coordinated patterns via low-rank representations, LoRA modifies how existing capabilities are applied without forcing the model to relearn basic tasks. The rank setting dictates the adapter's capacity and training overhead, allowing targeted modifications to components such as attention mechanisms while dramatically reducing parameter update costs.

items.title: How OpenAI Built GPT-Live
items.summary: Voice systems accept user audio as input and return an audio response to the listener. While the input and output modalities remain constant, the intermediary processing differs depending on system design. Historically, voice systems have evolved across three primary architectural generations. These generations comprise cascaded design, turn-based end-to-end models, and full-duplex architectures. The cascaded design for voice systems operates by sequentially chaining an automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, a large language model (LLM), and a text-to-speech (TTS) model. While each model handles the task it performs best, the architecture suffers from significant information loss because vocal nuances like tone and emotion are stripped from the transcript passed to the LLM. Furthermore, serial processing causes high cumulative latency, and managing three distinct components adds operational complexity. These shortcomings led to the development of second-generation turn-based speech-to-speech models. The second generation of voice systems introduces end-to-end speech-to-speech models that process audio directly, capturing vocal nuances lost in cascaded systems. However, interaction remains turn-based because it still relies on turn detectors and interruption mechanisms that frequently cause awkward pauses, cutoffs, or false triggers. Furthermore, these architectures are expensive to maintain because adopting new pre-trained foundation models requires retraining from scratch. These turn-taking challenges ultimately motivate the transition to third-generation full-duplex architectures.
